l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Polydore’s ghost reveals that Polymestor murdered him for the gold sent by Priam and left his corpse unburied on the Thracian shore. Hecuba learns that the Greek army has resolved to sacrifice Polyxena at Achilles’ tomb, and she unsuccessfully begs Ulysses to spare her daughter. Polyxena accepts her death rather than endure enslavement, and Ulysses leads her away to be killed. Hecuba is left grieving, enslaved, and fearful for the fate of her remaining son.

l: Polydore, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Polydore’s ghost says that Priam secretly sent him to Polymestor in Thrace with gold for his support. Polymestor murdered him for the gold and cast his body into the sea; Polydore returns so that Hecuba may give him burial.

l: Hecuba, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Hecuba, once queen of Troy, is now an aged captive who mourns her dead family. She tries to save Polyxena by appealing to Ulysses, but she is left to endure her daughter’s death and her own continued enslavement.

l: Polyxena, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Polyxena learns that the Greeks have voted to sacrifice her at Achilles’ tomb. She accepts death rather than risk being purchased as a slave or suffering dishonor, and she is led away by Ulysses.

l: Ulysses, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Ulysses tells Hecuba that the Greek army has ordered Polyxena’s death and that he has been commanded to escort her. He refuses Hecuba’s plea to spare her, arguing that Achilles must be honored, and leads Polyxena away.

l: Achilles, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Achilles’ ghost appears upon his tomb and demands that Polyxena be offered as a victim. The Greek army agrees to honor his request because he died nobly for Greece.

l: Polymestor, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Polymestor, ruler in the Thracian Chersonesus and Priam’s friend, fostered Polydore after Priam sent him away from Troy. After Troy fell, Polymestor killed Polydore for the gold entrusted to him.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: The Trojan captive dames serve as Hecuba’s attendants and chorus. They bring Hecuba news of the Greek decision to sacrifice Polyxena and sympathize with her grief.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: The Greek army remains encamped in the Thracian Chersonesus after Troy’s fall. It debates Achilles’ demand and resolves to give Polyxena as a sacrifice at his tomb.

l: Thracian Chersonesus, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: The Thracian Chersonesus is the coast where the Greek army is stationed after leaving Troy. It is also where Polymestor rules and where Polydore’s unburied corpse lies on the shore.

l: Thrace, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Thrace is the realm where Polymestor rules and where Polydore was raised after being sent away from Troy. Hecuba fears for Polydore, who is believed to be living there.

l: Troy, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Troy has been destroyed by the Greeks, and its royal family has been reduced to captivity or death. Hecuba recalls that its fall followed the deaths of Hector and Priam.

l: Achilles’ tomb, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Achilles’ tomb is the place where Polyxena is ordered to be sacrificed. Achilles’ ghost appears upon it and demands a Trojan captive as an offering.

l: Polydore’s corpse, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Polydore’s corpse has been cast into the sea and left unwept and unburied on the rocky shore. Polydore’s ghost seeks honorable burial and intends that Hecuba’s servant perform the rites.

l: Polyxena’s sacrifice, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Polyxena’s sacrifice is demanded by Achilles’ ghost and approved by the Greek army. Polyxena accepts it willingly, while Hecuba unsuccessfully attempts to take her place or prevent her death.

l: the fall and destruction of Troy, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: The fall of Troy brought the deaths of Hector and Priam, the destruction of the royal house, and the enslavement of the Trojan women. It also exposed Polydore to murder by Polymestor after his protection from Troy was no longer useful.

l: Polydore’s murder, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Polydore’s murder was committed by Polymestor, who wanted to keep the gold that Priam had sent with him. Polymestor then threw Polydore’s body into the sea.

l: Hecuba’s dream, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Hecuba dreams of a wolf tearing a dappled hind from her arms, and she understands the vision as a warning concerning Polydore and Polyxena. She also sees Achilles’ ghost demanding a Trojan captive.

l: the enslavement of Hecuba and the Trojan women, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Hecuba has been torn from the royal household and reduced to servitude after Troy’s destruction. She remains enslaved while Polyxena is taken away to die.

l: slavery, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Polyxena contrasts her former life as a free princess with the servitude that awaits her if she survives. She chooses death because she believes it preserves her freedom from dishonor and slavery.

l: death, Hecuba and other plays, HECUBA.
s: Death has taken Priam, Hector, and the other Trojan defenders, and it now awaits Polyxena. Hecuba remains alive to witness further deaths and describes continued life in captivity as a greater misery.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba learns from Talthybius that Polyxena was willingly sacrificed at Achilles’ tomb by the Greeks, who honored her courage and burial. Hecuba then receives Polyxena’s corse and orders that it be washed and properly adorned despite her captivity and poverty. An attendant brings the corse of Polydore, revealing that the Thracian king killed him after Priam had placed him in the king’s protection. The chorus recalls how Paris’s choice of Venus and his voyage from Sparta brought war, the destruction of Troy, and grief to the Greeks and Phrygians.

l: Hecuba, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba, formerly queen of Ilion and Priam’s wife, is reduced to an aged captive after Troy’s destruction. She mourns Polyxena and Polydore, praises Polyxena’s courage, orders that Polyxena’s corse be protected and washed, and laments the loss of her husband, children, city, and former status.

l: Polyxena, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Polyxena is sacrificed at Achilles’ tomb by the Greeks. She willingly faces death, refuses to be restrained, asks to be killed as one born free, and exposes her breast and neck for the fatal blow; afterward, the Greeks honor her with foliage, a pyre, and funeral offerings.

l: Polydore, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Polydore is Priam’s son, secretly placed by his aged father with the Thracian king for protection. The attendant finds his corse on the shore, and Hecuba concludes that the Thracian king murdered him for gold.

l: Talthybius, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Talthybius, herald of the Greeks, tells Hecuba how Polyxena was sacrificed. He describes Achilles’ son’s libations, the army’s silence, Polyxena’s courage, and the honors given to her corse, and he is instructed to prevent the Greeks from disturbing it.

l: Agamemnon, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon sends Talthybius to Hecuba and commands the Greek youths to release Polyxena when she asks to die freely. He later approaches while Hecuba and the chorus are discussing Polydore.

l: Priam, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Priam is described as the happy former king of Phrygia and the father of an illustrious race. He secretly placed Polydore with the Thracian king, and his city and household are destroyed in the Greek attack.

l: Paris, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Paris cuts down the pines on Ida and sails from Sparta to carry away the fairest bride. His actions are associated with the calamities that fall upon Troy and the Phrygian women.

l: Helen, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Helen is referred to as the fairest bride and as the Spartan virgin whose favored youth is untimely slain. She is also described as grieving beside the Eurotas and not sharing the victor’s pride.

l: Polymestor, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The Thracian king receives Polydore into his household after Priam entrusts him with the boy. He murders Polydore with a sword, apparently to possess the gold, violating the laws of hospitality.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The Greeks destroy Troy and hold Polyxena’s sacrifice at Achilles’ tomb. They obey the call for silence, release Polyxena when Agamemnon commands it, kill her, and then compete to honor her corse with foliage, a pyre, and funeral ornaments.

l: the Trojans, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The Trojans are represented through the destruction of their city and the loss of their royal household. Their homeland is conquered, their mansions are leveled, and the survivors are reduced to captivity and grief.

l: the Phrygian matrons, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The Phrygian women form the chorus and lament the destruction of Troy, the deaths of their sons, and their own enslavement. They recall Paris’s voyage and choice of Venus as the causes of the disasters that have overtaken them.

l: Troy, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Troy is described as conquered and sacked by the Greeks, with its bulwarks smoking and its mansions destroyed. Its former royal wealth and power have been reduced to captivity, mourning, and ruin.

l: Thrace, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Thrace is the place where Priam secretly entrusted Polydore to the Thracian king. The king’s household there becomes the setting for Polydore’s murder.

l: the Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The conflict is recalled through the Greek destruction of Troy, the deaths of its people, and the enslavement of its survivors. The chorus connects the war with Paris’s voyage from Sparta and his choice of Venus.

l: the sack of Troy, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The fall and sack of Troy leave Hecuba aged, childless, captive, and stripped of her former royal dignity. The city’s destruction is accompanied by the deaths of its men, the enslavement of its women, and the ruin of its palaces.

l: Polyxena’s sacrifice, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Polyxena’s sacrifice is performed by Achilles’ son at the sepulchral hillock of Achilles so that the Greeks may safely depart Troy. Polyxena accepts death freely, and the assembled Greeks honor her after she dies.

l: the judgment of Paris, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The chorus recalls that Paris judged three rival goddesses and awarded the prize to bright Venus. It presents this choice as the source of the woes that brought vengeance and war upon Troy.

l: Polydore’s murder, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Polydore’s murder is attributed to the Thracian king, who kills the boy entrusted to his protection in order to obtain gold. His corse is cast onto the shore, where an attendant finds it and brings it to Hecuba.

l: Fortune, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Fate is said to fulfill the commands of the immortal gods and to weigh the curse upon Priam’s house and Troy. Hecuba also reflects that human plans and boasts are vain because fortune can overturn prosperity.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba reveals to Agamemnon that the dead youth is her son, whom Polymestor murdered after Troy fell and whose body he cast into the sea. She begs Agamemnon to avenge the violation of hospitality and justice, but he fears blame from the Greek army. Agamemnon agrees to conceal Hecuba’s plan, restrain the Greeks if necessary, and allow the dead son and Polyxena to be buried together. Hecuba intends to use the captive Trojan women to punish Polymestor.

l: Agamemnon, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon learns from Hecuba that Polymestor murdered her son and cast his body into the sea. He pities Hecuba and wishes to avenge her, but fears that the Greeks will blame him for attacking their Thracian ally. He agrees to keep her plan secret, restrain the Greeks if they intervene, and permit the joint burial of her son and Polyxena.

l: Hecuba, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba identifies the dead youth as her son and begs Agamemnon to punish Polymestor for murdering him and denying him burial. She describes herself as a former queen who is now an enslaved, childless, cityless, and deeply afflicted woman. She plans to use the captive Trojan women to carry out her vengeance.

l: Polymestor, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Polymestor, the Thracian king and former friend of Hecuba, murdered her son after learning that Troy had fallen, apparently to seize the gold entrusted to him. He cast the youth’s body into the sea and failed to provide him a tomb. Hecuba plans to punish him.

l: Polydore, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba’s dead son had been sent to Polymestor for protection when Troy was destroyed. Polymestor murdered him for the gold and threw his mangled body into the sea, where a servant found it. Agamemnon agrees that his remains may be buried with Polyxena.

l: Polyxena, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Polyxena has been newly slain, and a servant was sent to fetch water to wash her remains. Hecuba asks Agamemnon to delay her interment so that she can be buried in the same fire and grave as Hecuba’s dead son.

l: Trojan women, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The captive Trojan women are concealed in the tents. Hecuba intends to enlist them in carrying out punishment against Polymestor.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Greeks regard Polymestor as an ally and Hecuba’s dead son as a foe. Agamemnon fears their blame if he openly attacks the Thracian king, while Hecuba asks him to restrain them if they try to defend Polymestor.

l: Ilion, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Ilion has been destroyed, and Hecuba sees its smoke rising. Its destruction prompts Polymestor to murder Hecuba’s son and leaves Hecuba enslaved and without a city.

l: revenge and retaliation, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba seeks vengeance against Polymestor for murdering her son and violating the obligations owed to a guest. She proposes that the captive Trojan women execute the plan, while Agamemnon secretly supports her and restrains opposition.

l: Justice, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba argues that the gods and justice require punishment for those who murder guests or violate sacred obligations. Agamemnon says he wishes to act according to the gods and justice, and the Chorus reflects that those who transgress should suffer.

l: funeral rites, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon says that the appropriate rites for Polyxena have been performed and agrees to delay her burial. He permits Polyxena and Hecuba’s dead son to be consumed in one fire and buried together.

l: Hecuba’s suffering, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba presents her suffering as unparalleled: she has lost her sons, her city, her royal status, and her freedom. She is now old, enslaved, and deprived of her children, with Polyxena newly dead and her remaining hope focused on vengeance.

l: women’s schemes, Hecuba and other plays, AGAMEMNON, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba claims that women’s wiles are difficult to resist and that their numbers can terrify an enemy. She intends to use these means, together with the Trojan women concealed in the tents, against Polymestor.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus laments Troy’s destruction and recalls how Hecuba escaped after seeing her husband dead and her native city ruined. Hecuba lures Polymestor into the Greek encampment by claiming that Priam’s treasure is hidden there, then has the Trojan women kill his sons and blinds him. Polymestor admits that he murdered Polydore to keep his gold and defends the act as protection against a renewed Trojan threat. Agamemnon hears both sides, judges Polymestor guilty, and orders him cast onto a deserted island, while Hecuba and the Trojan women prepare to bury the dead and depart for Greece.

l: Hecuba, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba deceives Polymestor by promising to reveal the location of Priam’s buried treasure. With the assistance of the Trojan women, she has Polymestor’s sons killed and blinds Polymestor, whom she holds responsible for murdering Polydore. She defends her revenge before Agamemnon, who accepts that Polymestor deserves punishment.

l: Polymestor, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Polymestor comes to Hecuba after returning from Thracia and admits that he murdered Polydore and kept the gold entrusted to him. Hecuba and the Trojan women kill his sons and blind him, after which he calls upon the Thracians and Grecian troops for help. Agamemnon rejects his justification and orders him cast onto a deserted island.

l: Agamemnon, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Agamemnon arrives after hearing Polymestor’s cries and hears the accounts of both Polymestor and Hecuba. He judges that Polymestor killed Polydore for the sake of the gold rather than to aid Greece, and orders him removed and cast onto a deserted island. He also orders that Polymestor’s sons’ corpses be buried.

l: Polydore, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Polydore was the youngest son of Priam and Hecuba, entrusted by his father to Polymestor for protection and upbringing. Polymestor murdered him after the fall of Troy so that he could retain Polydore’s gold and prevent him from restoring Troy.

l: sons of Polymestor, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Polymestor’s sons are present when Hecuba reveals the supposed location of Priam’s treasure. The Trojan women separate them from their father and kill them with concealed swords.

l: Trojan women, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The Trojan women assist Hecuba in killing Polymestor’s sons and blinding Polymestor. They later prepare to leave for their lords’ tents and endure the hardships imposed by their fate.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus laments Troy’s ruin and recalls Hecuba’s losses. It predicts Polymestor’s downfall, supports Hecuba’s cause, and observes that the severe suffering he has endured may excuse an assault on life.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Polymestor appeals to the Grecian troops and the sons of Atreus for assistance after being blinded and losing his sons. Agamemnon instead orders that Polymestor be removed from his sight.

l: Phrygia, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Troy is described as conquered, burned, and devastated, with its towers, palaces, streets, and native inhabitants lost. The Chorus laments that Troy will no longer stand conspicuously among impregnable fortresses.

l: Greece, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Greece is the destination toward which the surviving Trojan women and Agamemnon’s forces are preparing to sail. Polymestor claims that Polydore’s survival might have led Greece to invade Thrace again, but Hecuba rejects this as a pretext.

l: Greek encampment, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The Greek encampment contains the tents where the Trojan captives are held. Hecuba brings Polymestor into one of these tents under the pretense of showing him where treasure is concealed.

l: Priam’s treasure, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Polydore’s gold was brought from Troy and kept by Polymestor in his palace. Hecuba uses the promise of additional Priamite treasure to draw Polymestor into the tent, while Agamemnon concludes that greed for the gold motivated Polydore’s murder.

l: Polymestor’s sons’ corpses, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The corpses of Polymestor’s sons are left exposed after the Trojan women kill them. Agamemnon orders that both corpses be deposited in a grave.

l: the fall and destruction of Troy, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The fall of Troy leaves Hecuba, the Trojan women, and Polydore without their city and protection. Polymestor uses the fall as the occasion to murder Polydore, believing that a surviving son of Priam could gather Troy’s scattered citizens.

l: Polydore’s murder, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Polymestor confesses to the murder of Polydore, whom Priam had entrusted to him. Hecuba argues that he killed Polydore for gold and only after Troy had fallen, and Agamemnon finds this explanation convincing.

l: murder of Polymestor’s sons, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba arranges the murder of Polymestor’s sons as revenge for Polydore’s murder. The Trojan women hold Polymestor and stab his sons with swords concealed beneath their garments.

l: blinding of Polymestor, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba and the Trojan women blind Polymestor after killing his sons. He emerges from the tent unable to see, searches for his attackers, and appeals unsuccessfully to the Thracians and Grecian troops.

l: Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The Trojan War has ended with Troy’s towers overthrown and its city destroyed. The Greek forces are preparing to leave the captured land and return to their homes.

l: Justice, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba presents the killing of Polymestor’s sons and his blinding as a just atonement for his murder of Polydore. Agamemnon concludes that Polymestor deserves punishment because he murdered a protected guest for financial gain, and the Chorus associates his downfall with divine and human justice.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Amphitryon and Megara shelter with the children of Hercules at the altar of Jupiter because Lycus has seized Thebes and threatens to kill them. Lycus argues that Hercules was not truly courageous and orders that the family be burned, while Amphitryon and the Chorus defend Hercules’ honor and condemn Lycus’ tyranny. Megara accepts that death is unavoidable but asks to dress the children in funeral robes before their execution. Lycus allows them to enter Hercules’ house for this purpose, and Amphitryon reproaches Jove for failing to protect his son’s family.

l: Amphitryon, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Amphitryon identifies himself as Hercules’ father and describes Hercules’ lineage, labours, and descent to the Underworld. He shelters with Megara and the children at the altar of Jupiter, defends Hercules’ courage against Lycus, and begs that he and Megara be killed before the children. He finally reproaches Jove for sharing his nuptial couch yet failing to save Hercules’ family.

l: Megara, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Megara, the daughter of Creon and wife of Hercules, remains with Amphitryon and her children at the altar. She grieves for Hercules, recognizes that escape and persuasion are unlikely, and asks Lycus to let her dress the children in funeral robes before their threatened execution.

l: Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Hercules is described as the son of Jove and Amphitryon and the husband of Megara. He performed many labours, including killing the Hydra and the Nemean lion, but has descended to the Underworld and has not returned. Lycus threatens his family, while Amphitryon and the Chorus defend his courage and his services to Thebes and Greece.

l: Lycus, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Lycus has killed Creon, seized the throne of Thebes, and threatens to kill Megara, Amphitryon, and the children of Hercules. He disparages Hercules’ achievements and calls the bow a weapon of a coward. He orders wood to be gathered so the family can be burned, but permits Megara to enter Hercules’ house and dress the children before their deaths.

l: Jove, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Jove is presented as Hercules’ divine father and as the god whose altar protects the family. Amphitryon appeals to Jove to defend his son, then accuses him of being unjust or lacking wisdom because he has not saved Hercules’ children.

l: Creon, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Creon, the king of Thebes and Megara’s father, has been killed by Lycus. His death is the reason Lycus fears that the children of Hercules will later avenge him.

l: Chorus of Theban old men, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: The Chorus consists of aged Theban men who come to support Amphitryon, Megara, and the children. Though too weak to fight, they condemn Lycus as a foreign tyrant, defend Hercules’ honor, and declare that they will not willingly allow the children to be killed.

l: children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: The children shelter with Megara and Amphitryon at the altar of Jupiter and repeatedly ask when their father will return. Lycus orders their execution because he fears they will avenge Creon’s death, and Megara prepares to dress them in funeral robes.

l: Thebes, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Thebes is the city where Hercules’ house and the altar of Jupiter stand. Lycus has invaded it, killed Creon, and taken its throne, while the Chorus condemns the city for allowing a foreign ruler to govern it and for failing to protect Hercules’ family.

l: the Underworld, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: The Underworld is the realm to which Hercules has gone after entering through Taenarus to bring out the three-headed hound. Amphitryon and Megara fear that Hercules will not return, and Megara says that the dead do not normally come back from Pluto’s realm.

l: altar of Jupiter, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: The altar of Jupiter is the refuge where Amphitryon, Megara, and the children remain while threatened by Lycus. They lack food, drink, clothing, and shelter but continue to rely on the altar as their only protection.

l: Hercules’ house, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Hercules’ house in Thebes is closed against Megara, Amphitryon, and the children while Lycus threatens them. Lycus orders its gates opened so Megara can take the children inside and dress them in funeral robes before their execution.

l: the Labours of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: The Labours of Hercules include defeating the Hydra, killing the Nemean lion, overcoming other monsters, and purging the sea and land of dangers. Lycus minimizes these deeds, while Amphitryon presents them as evidence of Hercules’ greatness and courage.

l: Hercules’ descent to the Underworld, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Hercules descended through Taenarus to the realm of Pluto to bring the Underworld’s three-headed hound into the daylight. He has not yet returned, leaving his family exposed to Lycus.

l: the murder of Creon, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Lycus murdered Creon and then seized the throne of Thebes. He threatens Creon’s daughter Megara and her children because he fears that they will avenge Creon’s death when they grow older.

l: the attempted execution of Megara, Amphitryon, and the children, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Lycus threatens to kill Megara and the children of Hercules by burning them at the altar. He later allows them to enter Hercules’ house and put on funeral robes, after which he declares that he will send them to the Underworld.

l: tyranny, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Lycus embodies tyranny by seizing Thebes, silencing opposition, threatening the aged Chorus, and ordering the deaths of Megara and the children. The Chorus condemns him as an unworthy foreign ruler who governs through fear.

l: friendship and loyalty, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Amphitryon, Megara, and the Chorus remain loyal to Hercules and his children despite danger. Amphitryon observes that misfortune exposes false friends, while the Chorus insists that friends are needed even when the dead can no longer defend their families.

l: honor and reputation, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Amphitryon and the Chorus defend Hercules’ honor against Lycus’ accusation of cowardice. Amphitryon argues that skill with the bow can show prudence and courage, while Megara fears that dying in a shameful manner would dishonor their house.

l: Fortune, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES DISTRACTED.
s: Amphitryon hopes that fortune may change and save them, saying that storms and prosperity do not last forever. Megara counters that what fate ordains cannot be prevented and that resisting necessity may be folly.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus praises Hercules and recounts his many labours, including slaying the Nemean lion, the Centaurs, the Hydra, Geryon, and other monsters, and capturing Diomedes’ horses. It describes Hercules’ journey to the Hesperian gardens, the Euxine, and the underworld. Hercules has entered Pluto’s mansion, where the Chorus fears that he and his sons face an eternal fate. Hercules’ wife, his sons, and his aged father are seen in funereal vestments, and the Chorus mourns them.

l: Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hercules is praised for his matchless fortitude and for completing many labours. He slew numerous monsters, captured Diomedes’ horses, defeated the Amazons, and entered the underworld.

l: the Labours of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hercules’ labours include killing the Nemean lion, wounding the Centaurs, capturing the golden-horned hind and Diomedes’ horses, defeating Cycnus, killing the dragon of the Hesperian gardens, relieving Atlas, defeating the Amazons, subduing the Hydra, and killing Geryon.

l: children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hercules’ sons are seen being conducted in funereal vestments with Hercules’ wife and his aged father. The Chorus says that the boat of Charon waits to bear them to their eternal home.

l: Megara, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hercules’ loved wife is seen in funereal vestments conducting Hercules’ sons together with his decrepit father. The Chorus mourns while looking upon them.

l: Hercules’ death, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: Hercules comes to Pluto’s mansion, called the house of tears and the goal of labour, where he is not expected to return. The Chorus describes his friends as dismayed and mourns his fate.

l: the Underworld, Hecuba and other plays, CHORUS.
s: The underworld is described as Pluto’s mansion, a place of gloomy shades and tears. Its stern law is pronounced, and the boat of Charon waits to carry the dead to their eternal home.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Megara laments that she, her children, and Amphitryon are being forced toward death and imagines them as victims destined for Pluto’s realm. She recalls Hercules’ former promises that his sons would inherit Argos, Thebes, and Oecalia, while her plans for their marriages have been destroyed. Megara calls on the deceased Hercules to appear and protect his family, but Amphitryon declares that they must die and appeals unsuccessfully to Zeus. Amphitryon tells the Chorus that Fortune has suddenly stripped him of his former glory and urges the aged men to make the best use of their remaining lives.

l: Megara, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Megara mourns that she, her children, and the aged Amphitryon are being led together to death. She recalls the hopes Hercules had formed for his sons’ inheritances and marriages, calls on Hercules to protect them, and says that their murderers are cowards compared with him.

l: Amphitryon, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Amphitryon raises his hands to the sky and appeals to Zeus to save the deserted children, but he believes that his prayers have failed and that they must die. He tells the Chorus that Fortune has taken away his former glory in a single day and bids them make life as pleasant as possible while it lasts.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus consists of aged men whom Amphitryon addresses as his comrades. He urges them to cast off grief and live as sweetly as they can because time abandons human hopes.

l: Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Hercules is described as deceased and absent while his father, children, and Megara face death. Megara calls on him to hear them from Pluto’s realm and appear, even as a ghost, because his presence would be enough to protect his children.

l: children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Hercules’ sons are being prepared as victims for death and are forced to descend to Pluto’s abode with Megara and Amphitryon. Their father had hoped that they would inherit Argos, Thebes, and Oecalia, but those hopes have proved false.

l: Fortune, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Changeful Fortune has assigned the Destinies as brides to Megara’s children, replacing the marriages she had planned. Amphitryon says that Fortune has taken all his former glory from him in a single day.

l: fate and the Destinies, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: The Destinies are presented as the brides whom changeful Fortune has given to the children in place of their intended consorts. Their coming marriage is associated with tears and death rather than happiness.

l: inveterate foes, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Megara says that she bore and nurtured her children only for them to become the scorn and sport of their inveterate foes, who are to cause their deaths.

l: death, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Death is described as an unseemly force that carries Megara, her children, and Amphitryon away together. The family is destined to descend to Pluto’s realm, and Amphitryon concludes that they must die.

l: the attempted execution of Megara, Amphitryon, and the children, Hecuba and other plays, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: The children’s sacrifice is imminent: Megara asks what priest or butcher will slay them or pierce her breast, and says that the victims are already prepared for descent to Pluto’s abode. She portrays the sacrifice as a forced, collective death involving the children, herself, and Amphitryon.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Hercules returns from the Underworld with Cerberus and finds Megara, Amphitryon, and his children dressed for their impending deaths under Lycus’s rule. After learning that Lycus killed Megara’s brothers and intends to kill his family, Hercules hides in the palace and vows vengeance. Hercules kills Lycus inside the palace, and the Chorus celebrates the tyrant’s downfall and the restoration of justice. The unit ends with the Chorus seeing a frightening spectre hovering over the palace.

l: Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Hercules returns safely from the Underworld and is astonished to find Megara, his children, and Amphitryon in funeral garments. After learning that Lycus intends to kill them, he hides in the palace, vows to avenge his family, and kills Lycus.

l: Megara, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Megara recognizes Hercules when he returns and tells him that Lycus has killed her brothers and threatens her, her children, and Amphitryon. She enters the palace with Hercules and the children after he promises to protect them.

l: Amphitryon, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Amphitryon welcomes Hercules and explains the danger posed by Lycus and his supporters. He urges Hercules to remain hidden in the palace, then leaves expecting Lycus to be killed and rejoicing in the tyrant’s deserved punishment.

l: Lycus, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Lycus rules Thebes after seizing the sceptre through revolt and orders Megara, Amphitryon, and the children to appear for execution. He enters the palace to bring them out but is killed there by Hercules.

l: children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: The children are dressed in funeral garments and cling tightly to Hercules when he returns. Hercules carries them into the palace to protect them from Lycus.
